nonBlocking: Deleted-path fallback still diverges between languages when the parent directory is also gone: Swift returns the raw absolute path (NFC) while Python's os.path.realpath resolves as many leading components as it can. Pre-existing, not introduced here; a record for such a path is unlikely to exist, but documenting or aligning the two fallbacks would close the gap.

Records previously written by Swift under an NFD key for non-ASCII paths are orphaned, as the patch notes. The stale <key>.json/<key>.lock pairs are never cleaned up. Acceptable for a historical cache; consider a one-line note in the release log so operators know to run --rehash-model for non-ASCII model paths.

The new coverage uses a Latin accent (U+00E8). The triggering case was a Korean filename, whose NFD form is algorithmic Hangul jamo decomposition. Both Foundation and unicodedata implement this per the standard, but adding one Hangul spelling pair to the Swift and Python tests would pin the actual reported case.

Swift String == uses canonical equivalence, so the record.path == canonical guard in readRecord would pass for NFC/NFD mismatches by design. This is harmless now that every stored path is NFC and the key is byte-exact, and the test correctly compares utf8 byte arrays, but a byte-level comparison in readRecord would make the mismatch check as strict as the Python side.

test_record_format_and_key compares against os.path.realpath without NFC. Correct for ASCII temp dirs on macOS, but would fail if the test root ever contained non-ASCII characters. Using mdc.canonical_path there keeps the test robust.

NFC results could in principle differ between Foundation's ICU tables and Python's unicodedata for characters added in a newer Unicode version than one of the two supports. Not reachable for Hangul or Latin accents; worth a comment only.

Final Swift build and the 2042-test suite are reported as in progress. The Swift test additions depend on existing helpers (check, checkEqual, lowerHex, SHA256.hash over [UInt8], root, fm, abc, abcd) matching their prior accepted signatures. If that run fails, re-review the failing assertions before shipping.
rationale: The correction is minimal and addresses the real defect: the cache key depended on spelling because realpath(3) reports the on-disk (NFD on HFS+, stored form on APFS) spelling for an existing file while the deleted-file fallback kept the caller's spelling, so a non-ASCII model's key drifted across deletion and between Swift and Python. Applying NFC on every branch of canonicalPath and to Python's realpath result makes the key a pure function of the resolved path's canonical form, and both sides hash the UTF-8 of that NFC string. The follow-on change to open the caller's URL/path for the single streaming hash is necessary and correct: the NFC canonical string is no longer guaranteed to be an on-disk name, and the caller's spelling is by definition openable. Cache semantics are intact: a hit reads the record under the per-key flock, performs no stat/mtime/size check, and never touches model bytes; a miss hashes exactly once; refresh is explicit only; malformed, mismatched, or retired-policy records throw with the refresh instruction and are never silently rehashed or returned as a digest. ASCII paths are fixed points under NFC, so the real model's historical seed, key, and record are byte-identical. The new tests cover key equality across NFC/NFD spellings before and after deletion, NFC storage of the record path, hit-without-read after mutation and deletion, and both cross-format record readings. No weights or credentials are included. Acceptance is contingent on the in-progress Swift build and test run completing green.
